**The Worst Haircut Experience of My Life!**

The salon in question is a place that's been hyped within our community as a haven for African American haircare. They've positioned themselves as experts in textured hair, promising to understand the unique needs of our curls, coils, and locs. But what they've delivered is far from the promised "cultural understanding" and "tailored care."

From the moment I walked in, the atmosphere was warm and inviting, which initially made me feel at ease. The staff seemed friendly enough, but as I sat in the chair, I began to notice some red flags. The stylist, who barely exchanged more than a few words with me, started cutting my hair without any real conversation or understanding of my hair type. It was clear they were rushing through the process, more interested in getting me out the door than actually providing a good service.

The "stylist" (who I now question if they even have proper training) took my straight hair and turned it into a chop job that could only be described as a butchering. They used techniques that were clearly not suited for my hair texture, leaving my edges jagged and my hair looking more like a mess than a styled masterpiece. The ends were so dried out and split that I couldn't even run my fingers through my own hair without causing pain.

What really hurt was the price tag. I was charged an arm and a leg for a service that left my hair in worse condition than when I walked in. They tried to justify it by saying it's "expensive because it's organic and high-quality," but I'm not paying premium prices for a service that didn't even deliver on their basic promises. It's like taking your car to a mechanic, paying through the roof, and having them treat your vehicle like it's a junkyard car.

Even worse, when I expressed my concerns, they dismissed me, acting like I was the problem. They had the audacity to tell me that I should've known what I was getting into and that I was "too sensitive" for mentioning their mistakes. It's a tactic designed to silence people of color into accepting subpar treatment, but it won't work here.

Or how the "consultation" I paid for was nothing more than a 5-minute chat where they asked few questions and seemed lost. But the broader issue here is the exploitation of our community. This salon is preying on the desire for us to feel seen and validated, only to take advantage of our trust.

If you value your hair, your money, and your dignity, I beg you to run, don’t let them take your money. This place is a masterclass in exploitation. They don't care about our community; they care about your dollars. There are better salons out there that respect and understand the complexities of our hair, and I will never again trust someone who disrespects the very people they're supposed to be serving.

In the end, this wasn't just a bad hair day—it was a betrayal. And I'll be sure to share this experience with everyone I know, so you all can avoid the same fate.<｜end▁of▁sentence｜>
